title: Product Detail Photos: Close-Ups of Texture | AIVideosUGC
description: Turn one sharp photo into a close-up of stitching, grain, hardware, or finish. Use these product detail photos in a listing gallery and in paid ads.
h1: Product Detail Photos of Stitching, Grain and Finish
lead: Shoppers paying more can see the stitch, grain, or clasp up close, instead of a prettier table. Pick a tight crop from the wall and use a photo where that detail is already sharp.

steps.d: Use the listing photo focused on the stitch and painted edge. The tight crop keeps attention on the paint.
Tell the buyer the paint keeps the edge from opening up in a pocket. That plain line is what they hear.
Place a 1:1 of the painted edge after the full wallet photo in the gallery. A 15-second clip costs 60 credits, shown first.

faq.q: What is a product detail template?
faq.a: A product detail template is a ready-made close-up for one feature, such as stitching, grain, or a clasp. You add a sharp photo of that spot, and the crop holds it still long enough to judge.

faq.q: How does a detail template become a video?
faq.a: Use the sharp feature photo, name what it does, and place a square after the full product shot. A shopper can see the detail without being told to look harder.

faq.q: Why use this instead of booking a macro shoot?
faq.a: You skip a half day of macro filming and the fee that comes with it. The listing already has a sharp frame, so a price change can go live with the close-up you have.

faq.q: Who is a detail template for?
faq.a: Shops that sell how a product is built, not a logo slapped on a box. A bag seller who answers hardware questions in the comments is the usual person here.

faq.q: Can a beginner make a close-up ad?
faq.a: Yes. Someone who has only ever posted phone photos can make the close-up. They pick the crop. The sharp photo decides the frame.
Jewelry clasps, bag hardware, and a fabric weave all fit when the photo is already sharp on that spot. A wide lifestyle shot where the clasp is a speck does not.

faq.q: Can I use my own detail photo, a clip, and a logo?
faq.a: Yes. Use the detail photo you already have, even when the logo sits in the corner. A clip of a finger running along the feature can be the motion, so you do not need a separate logo file to start.

faq.q: Where can I place the close-up, and in what size?
faq.a: The product page, YouTube, a Story, and a banner each have a size. A 1:1 belongs on the product page after the full shot. YouTube can take 16:9 if the detail should travel. A Story wants 9:16 at 6 or 10 seconds, and 4:3 or 3:4 covers a banner. 15 and 30 seconds are there for a slower pass along the detail.

faq.q: Do I need a paid plan to use a template?
faq.a: Yes. Starter is $24.50 a month with 200 credits, Pro is $35 with 300, and Premium is $63 with 600. A photo spends 24 credits. A 6, 10, 15, or 30 second clip spends 24, 40, 60, or 120 credits. The total shows before the run, and a failed run gives those credits back.

faq.q: Can I use the close-up commercially and for clients?
faq.a: Yes. Run the close-up as an ad and hand the same file to a client for a listing. The export has no watermark.

faq.q: What does a product detail template include?
faq.a: The crop and the moment the feature appears are already chosen. You name the feature in words a buyer actually uses, such as the grain or the weave.

steps.prompt: Show the uploaded wallet’s stitched edge and grain in a crisp square close-up.

reviews.h2: How Shops Use a Detail Close-Up
reviews.lead: One feature fills the picture, taken from a sharp photo. A voice or a presenter can point at that same feature.

items.d: A bag shop enlarges a handle stitch so the thread fills the square, then checks it against the source.
A belt shop brings the leather grain forward from a sharp photo, then makes a short clip from that same photo.
A wallet shop has an AI actor point at a painted edge that already fills the picture.
A jewelry shop enlarges the clasp and shortens the spoken line in the built-in editor.
A shoe shop shows the sole seam and the stitching, then a voice in another language for a second market.
A watch shop enlarges the side knob and edits the script without leaving the page.
A jacket shop uses an AI actor beside zipper teeth that fill the picture.
A home shop makes a tabletop grain close-up from a photo that already showed the surface, with no new light setup.
A hardware shop pastes the product link, enlarges a metal knob, and makes a second version.
An apparel shop types the bottom seam, keeps the full garment photo first, and checks the close-up.

items.t: A Read Voice or a Clone
items.d: A stock voice, or a clone from a short sample, can name the feature out loud.
You can change the sentences so they stay on the stitch, grain, or clasp shoppers should notice. Draft from your note or the product link.

items.t: An AI Avatar at the Detail
items.d: An AI avatar can point at the feature, so you do not book a macro day. Add B-roll that stays tight on the material when the ad needs more than a face.
Paste the listing to start a script. Shop software can send the feature photo through the API.
A buyer in Mexico can read the weave note in Spanish on the same scarf photo. The caption can move so it stays off the pattern.
A second feature or a second market comes from the same photo, ready to post. Publish through a connected account to Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, or TikTok, or download the file.
